Neonatal Sand goannas emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a developmental period that depends heavily on incubation temperature. Experiments using artificial incubation regimes have demonstrated that eggs maintained at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C] require approximately 335 days [ab = approximately 335 days] to complete development and hatch. This remarkably protracted incubation period, exceeding eleven months, stands in contrast to the much shorter durations observed at higher temperatures and reflects the profound metabolic suppression imposed by cool conditions. At the moment of hatching, these young-of-year reptiles exhibit a wet weight at birth of 26 grams [Wwb = 26 grams], a figure derived from measurements on captive-bred individuals and consistent with the general pattern observed in the closely related Nile monitor, Varanus niloticus. This modest neonatal mass belies the substantial growth trajectory that lies ahead as these ectothermic predators begin their transition from lecithotrophic dependence on internal yolk reserves to the active pursuit of invertebrate and small vertebrate prey.

As these hatchlings grow and mature, they undergo a period of rapid mass gain that ultimately carries them toward their maximum adult body size. Field records and data from long-term mark-recapture studies indicate that the largest individuals of Varanus gouldii attain an ultimate wet weight of 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams]. This substantial adult body mass, equivalent to roughly 6 kilograms, positions the species as a moderately large varanid, although it remains considerably smaller than its formidable relatives such as the perentie or the Komodo dragon. Reaching this upper size limit requires several years of consistent foraging and thermoregulatory effort, with the peak mass typically recorded in dominant, well-fed adults that have secured access to productive home ranges. The species exhibits no pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this regard, with both sexes capable of approaching this asymptotic mass under favorable conditions, though females tend to invest heavily in somatic growth before directing resources toward egg production.

The metabolic machinery that supports this impressive growth and activity has been quantified through laboratory-based respirometry trials. Measurements of resting oxygen consumption conducted at a standard body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 1.9 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 1.9 milliliters of oxygen per minute]. This value, representing the energetic cost of maintaining basic physiological functions in a post-absorptive, inactive state, is typical for a reptile of this body size and reflects the characteristically low metabolic intensity of ectotherms compared with endotherms of equivalent mass. The measurement was obtained from individuals acclimated to warm conditions, ensuring that the recorded rate represents a true basal state unconfounded by the thermal hysteresis or cold-induced metabolic depression that can complicate interpretation in varanid lizards. Such data provide a critical baseline for modeling the daily energetic costs of foraging, digestion, and reproduction in this active predator.

Reproductive activity in the Sand goanna is tightly linked to seasonal temperature cues, with females typically producing a single clutch of eggs per year under the warm conditions of the austral spring and summer. The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been documented in populations experiencing a mean ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], where females deposit up to 15 eggs in a single clutch [N_R_i = up to 15 eggs in a single clutch]. This clutch, laid within a carefully excavated nest burrow, represents a substantial energetic investment for the gravid female. The frequency of these events is constrained to approximately one clutch annually [F_R_i = approximately one clutch annually], reflecting the extended period required for follicular development, vitellogenesis, and subsequent oviposition. Under these thermal conditions, the effective daily reproduction rate derived from combining these values underscores the species' reliance on high fecundity per event rather than on frequent, iteroparous nesting attempts, a strategy well suited to the unpredictable rainfall patterns of its arid and semi-arid habitats.

Life-history milestones in Varanus gouldii are achieved over a timeframe that reflects the slow pace typical of large-bodied varanids. Females attain sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gonadal activation and the first production of viable oocytes, at approximately 3 years following the hatching event [tp = approximately 3 years following the hatching event], a duration estimated from studies of the closely related Rosenberg's goanna, Varanus rosenbergi, under field conditions averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This delay before the first reproductive effort allows females to accumulate the necessary body condition and fat reserves to support the high energetic demands of egg production. The species' overall maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at roughly 18.3 years [am = roughly 18.3 years], again based on records from populations operating at a mean temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though captive individuals may exceed this figure under protected conditions. This combination of delayed maturation, modest annual fecundity, and considerable longevity points to a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival across multiple breeding seasons in a challenging environment.
